1.content: Create a native desktop app with Rust and open your first window.

2.content: macOS 14 or later Rust 1.90 or later Bun 1.4 or later Xcode Command Line Tools ( xcode-select --install ) macOS is the supported target today.

3.content: init writes the project and installs dependencies. Omit --language to choose Go, TypeScript, or Rust interactively.

4.content: The generated src/main.rs opens a window. Keep state on your View and call cx.invalidate() after you change it. on_reopen opens a window again when the user clicks the Dock icon and none are visible.

5.content: dev rebuilds as you edit. build writes a packaged app under dist/ .

6.content: Write components . Keep them in sync with view state . Add styles and layout .

7.content: The files in a QuickGUI Rust project and how to configure them. A Rust project keeps application code in a Cargo package and development commands in a small Bun package.

8.content: Commit Cargo.lock after the first successful build. Split larger apps into ordinary Rust modules.

9.content: src/main.rs starts Application::new().run(...) and opens windows from that callback. Each window owns a View . entry in the config is the crate directory.

10.content: TOML supports the same keys. The CLI reads quickgui.toml before quickgui.config.ts . Enable optional crate features in Cargo.toml instead of setting extensions in the app config.

11.content: Applications depend on the quickgui crate. @quickgui/cli is a development dependency. Optional terminal and updater capabilities are Cargo features. Keep the crate version already in your project:

13.content: Write views, compose children, and use the built-in control set. Implement View for screens that keep state. Functions that return Element work for stateless pieces.

14.content: Child views can also be functions that return Element when they have no state of their own.

15.content: div , text , button , text_input , text_area , Markdown , img , svg , custom_shader , and VirtualList are the building blocks. submit_button submits the nearest form . Terminal is available behind a crate feature.

16.content: Keep parts under the root they belong to so focus and values stay connected.

17.content: Store values on the view, pass them into constructors, and update them from listeners. Then call cx.invalidate() . The view owns the state.

18.content: The component reference covers forms, overlays, menus, tables, trees, and more. examples/base_ui_components.rs is a gallery.

19.content: Apply fluent style methods on each visible part. Parts ship unstyled so colors and layout belong to your app. Types such as TabsState and SelectState expose the current state for custom presentation.

20.content: Store view state and redraw when it changes. Store state on the View . render reads that state to build elements. Call cx.invalidate() after a mutation so the window redraws.

21.content: Keep fields on the view struct. Register listeners with cx.listener so events can mutate those fields. A value you copy in render is the current frame’s snapshot.

22.content: Compute derived values in render from the fields you already store. Store an expensive derivation on the view when several children need the same value in one frame.

23.content: Start external work from listeners or Application callbacks, and stop it when the view is dropped. Closing a window drops the view and its listeners.

24.content: Calling cx.invalidate() marks the window dirty. Multiple invalidations in one event become one render. Do not install a timer to redraw when nothing changed.

25.content: Show and hide content, render lists, and work with the current window. View::render builds the UI after you invalidate or the operating system asks for a redraw. Use id so rows keep their identity across renders.

26.content: Return impl IntoElement from render . The window sleeps until invalidate or a platform event.

27.content: Omitting a branch drops those nodes.

28.content: Give stateful rows stable id s. For long collections, use VirtualList or Table .

29.content: Each open_window owns an independent view. Closing one window does not drop the others. Handle the Dock icon by opening a new window when has_visible_windows is false.

31.content: examples/base_ui_components.rs is the UI gallery. Enable the inspector crate feature for the in-app inspector.

32.content: Lay out and style views with Flexbox, Grid, and interaction states. Fluent methods set layout, paint, typography, and interaction styles. Lengths are logical pixels.

33.content: Presets such as flex_col , p_3 , rounded_lg , and text_lg match the Go and TypeScript helpers. p_3 is 12 pixels. For custom values, use rounded(10.0) , p(14.0) , and w / h .

37.content: Use grid plus track, placement, and span methods.

38.content: Font family, weight, size, wrapping, and selection apply to text. Colors accept Color::rgb8 , Color::rgba8 , and packed values.

40.content: Name a group on an ancestor and use group_hover on descendants so they style together.

41.content: Build text fields, checkboxes, radios, and select controls. Pass the current value into text_input / text_area and write edits from on_input .

43.content: Field and Fieldset connect labels, descriptions, controls, and errors. Validation lives on FieldState .

44.content: Compose Checkbox , CheckboxGroup , RadioGroup , Radio , and Switch with their indicators and labels. Store checked values on the view and update them from listeners.

45.content: SelectState , ComboboxState , and AutocompleteState hold the current value and options. Keep option values stable.

46.content: Input listeners receive the next text. Register pointer, key, and submit handlers on ViewContext .

47.content: Show popovers, dialogs, and operating-system file pickers. Use a QuickGUI overlay for app-styled content, or a system dialog for file picking and alerts.

48.content: Compose trigger, positioner, popup, and arrow parts. Store open on the view.

50.content: SystemPopover opens a native child window, which can extend past the owner window’s edge.

52.content: Declare routes, nested layouts, and in-app navigation. Declare routes, render the match in the current window, and navigate with push / replace .

53.content: RouteDefinition::layout declares a pathless ancestor. Relative child paths join their parent; an absolute child path starts at the root.

54.content: Match the route chain and wrap inner content with layout elements. Pathless layouts appear in the match without adding a URL segment.

55.content: The controller supports push , replace , back , and forward . Navigation stays inside the app.

57.content: Animate hover, color, and opacity, and play GIF or WebP images. Animate style changes with transition . The view does not rebuild for each frame.

59.content: Change a style field from view state and call invalidate . Keep the element mounted while it animates.

60.hierarchy: Transitions & Animation › Timing and frame rate
60.content: Transition::new takes a Duration . Set easing with with_easing and optionally cap cadence with max_fps .

61.content: Background, border color and width, radius, text color, box shadow, opacity, and transform interpolate. Width, height, and padding do not.

62.hierarchy: Transitions & Animation › Mounting and reduced motion
62.content: Keep an overlay mounted during its exit transition when the component supports that. Transitions follow the system Reduce Motion setting.

63.content: img plays GIF and WebP files from the path you pass. You do not need a timer.

64.content: Open windows and use menus, clipboard, dialogs, and file watching. Call Application::new().run(...) once from main . Its startup callback creates windows.

65.content: cx.open_window(WindowOptions::new("Title").size(width, height), view) creates a window with its own View . Closing the window drops that view. Handle the Dock icon with Application::on_reopen when has_visible_windows is false.

66.hierarchy: Windows & Native Services › Commands and services
66.content: Typed APIs cover dialogs, clipboard, shell, appearance, menus, and displays. Capture cx.window_handle() during a listener when later work needs that window.

67.hierarchy: Windows & Native Services › Events and file watching
67.content: Window events include focus, resize, appearance, minimize, fullscreen, and close. Application callbacks include reopen, activation, quit, and open URLs. Enable the file-watcher crate feature when you need filesystem events, and drop watchers with the owning view.

68.content: Embed real SwiftUI controls inside a Rust application. Enable the swift-ui crate feature. Ordinary QuickGUI components work without it.

69.content: Construct MacSwiftUiHost , sync a descriptor tree, and mount it with native_view .

70.content: Buttons, toggles, sliders, steppers, progress views, gauges, text and secure fields, pickers, segmented controls, date and color pickers, and popovers.

74.content: Style SwiftUI controls and nest QuickGUI content inside them. Apply SwiftUiModifier values in declaration order. Convenience builders such as style , control_size , and disabled append those modifiers.

76.content: macOS draws glass where it is available.

79.content: Dropping MacSwiftUiHost releases the native view. A presented panel closes with its owner.

80.content: Ship signed automatic updates for macOS, Windows, and Linux. Enable the updater feature on the quickgui crate. Rust apps call UpdateClient directly.

81.content: Generate a signing key pair and copy the public key into the project: Keep the private quickgui-update.key out of version control. Enable the crate feature. Keep the crate version already in your project: The CLI embeds the public key, version, identifier, and feed URL. A darwin-arm64 build checks https://downloads.example.com/my-app/appcast-darwin-arm64.xml unless you set updates.feedUrl .

82.content: Construct one UpdateClient after the application starts, outside View::render : A Check for Updates action can call check from a listener and cx.invalidate() when UI should show progress.

83.content: Keep the client for the process lifetime. Closing a window must not drop it if other windows still need update status.

84.content: macOS can emit Sparkle appcasts when updates.publicKey is set. Windows and Linux use signed JSON manifests. Point development builds at a disposable feed.

85.content: Signing needs the private key in updates.minisignSecretKey or QUICKGUI_MINISIGN_SECRET_KEY . The private key is never embedded in the application.

86.content: Packaged Rust apps include the executable and quickgui.json . The updater reads the embedded public key and current version from that metadata.

87.content: Share Rust modules or author a native service for Go and TypeScript apps. A Rust app can share ordinary modules, or it can author a native extension that Go and TypeScript apps load. Rust apps enable crate features instead of listing extensions in config.

88.content: What you are adding What you ship Components or application logic A Rust module or crate Optional QuickGUI capabilities Cargo features such as updater and terminal A native service for Go or TypeScript A cdylib , a manifest, and a typed wrapper A Rust app already links quickgui . It does not load a separate host library.

89.content: Use this when Go or TypeScript apps should consume a native service. --npm-package sets the artifact package name.

90.content: Export functions that return Element : Return notice("Saved") as a child. Keep application-wide services outside View::render .

91.hierarchy: Authoring Extensions › Lay out a native extension
91.content: A native extension ships quickgui.extension.json , a versioned shared library, and declared resources. Rust extensions can vendor extension_api.rs and build a cdylib without linking the renderer. See the Go Authoring Extensions guide for the native contract.

92.content: Rust applications enable features in Cargo.toml . Keep the crate version already in your project: Go and TypeScript consumers declare the extension package in their own config.

93.hierarchy: Authoring Extensions › Implement the native contract
93.content: Implement invoke and shutdown . Copy borrowed input before returning, keep events scoped to their sessions, and release workers when a session stops.

94.content: Go and TypeScript CLIs bundle declared extensions. A Rust app has nothing extra to register: Cargo links the crates you depend on.

95.hierarchy: Authoring Extensions › Build and package artifacts
95.content: App edits rebuild the selected crate. Rebuild an extension when its native implementation changes, then rebuild the consuming Go or TypeScript app.

96.content: Test a packed cdylib with the generated demo app. Rust applications call crate APIs directly instead of invokeExtension .

141.content: Checkbox pub fn new(state: impl Into<ToggleState>) -> Self parent pub fn parent(children: impl IntoIterator<Item = bool>) -> Self Derive a parent checkbox from the checked values of the boxes it governs. This is Base UI's `parent` checkbox: every child checked reports on, none reports off, and a mix reports mixed. QuickGUI keeps no child registry — the application passes the values it is already rendering — so the derivation stays a pure function of the caller's own data. ``` use quickgui::{Checkbox, ToggleState}; assert_eq!(Checkbox::parent([true, true]).state(), ToggleState::On); assert_eq!(Checkbox::parent([false, false]).state(), ToggleState::Off); assert_eq!(Checkbox::parent([true, false]).state(), ToggleState::Mixed); // An empty group is unchecked rather than mixed. assert_eq!(Checkbox::parent([]).state(), ToggleState::Off); ``` read_only pub const fn read_only(mut self, read_only: bool) -> Self Show a value the user may read but not change, Base UI's `readOnly`. Unlike a disabled checkbox, a read-only one stays focusable and stays in the Tab sequence. QuickGUI projects the state and refuses the transition through [`Self::next_state`]; the application's own listener asks for that transition rather than toggling blindly. state pub const fn state(self) -> ToggleState Configures state for this part. is_read_only pub const fn is_read_only(self) -> bool Configures is read only for this part. next_state pub const fn next_state(self) -> Option<ToggleState> The state an activation moves this checkbox to, or `None` when it refuses. Mixed and off both move to on, and on moves to off, which is the web's tri-state contract. A read-only checkbox returns `None`, so a click listener that asks before writing cannot change a value the control is refusing. parent_next_checked pub const fn parent_next_checked(self) -> Option<bool> The checked value activating a parent checkbox moves its whole group to. A partially or fully unchecked parent checks everything; a fully checked one clears it. Returns `None` when the parent is read-only. Checkbox pub fn new(state: impl Into<ToggleState>) -> Self parent pub fn parent(children: impl IntoIterator<Item = bool>) -> Self Derive a parent checkbox from the checked values of the boxes it governs. This is Base UI's `parent` checkbox: every child checked reports on, none reports off, and a mix reports mixed. QuickGUI keeps no child registry — the application passes the values it is already rendering — so the derivation stays a pure function of the caller's own data. ``` use quickgui::{Checkbox, ToggleState}; assert_eq!(Checkbox::parent([true, true]).state(), ToggleState::On); assert_eq!(Checkbox::parent([false, false]).state(), ToggleState::Off); assert_eq!(Checkbox::parent([true, false]).state(), ToggleState::Mixed); // An empty group is unchecked rather than mixed. assert_eq!(Checkbox::parent([]).state(), ToggleState::Off); ``` read_only pub const fn read_only(mut self, read_only: bool) -> Self Show a value the user may read but not change, Base UI's `readOnly`. Unlike a disabled checkbox, a read-only one stays focusable and stays in the Tab sequence. QuickGUI projects the state and refuses the transition through [`Self::next_state`]; the application's own listener asks for that transition rather than toggling blindly. state pub const fn state(self) -> ToggleState Configures state for this part. is_read_only pub const fn is_read_only(self) -> bool Configures is read only for this part. next_state pub const fn next_state(self) -> Option<ToggleState> The state an activation moves this checkbox to, or `None` when it refuses. Mixed and off both move to on, and on moves to off, which is the web's tri-state contract. A read-only checkbox returns `None`, so a click listener that asks before writing cannot change a value the control is refusing. parent_next_checked pub const fn parent_next_checked(self) -> Option<bool> The checked value activating a parent checkbox moves its whole group to. A partially or fully unchecked parent checks everything; a fully checked one clears it. Returns `None` when the parent is read-only.
